title: Kakudmi waits one song
hook: a king waits through one song in Brahma's hall, and ages pass on earth
carry: time is a wheel of ages, lived one instant at a time
tomorrow: a young sage the bathers didn't hide from

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mudgala sent heaven's chariot away. Heaven isn't the goal; freedom is.

In the Bhagavata Purana, a king named Kakudmi has a daughter, Revati, and he can't find anyone good enough for her. So he does what only a king of old could do. He takes her up to Brahma's own world, to ask the creator himself. When they arrive, Brahma is listening to the heavenly musicians, so father and daughter wait politely until the song ends. Then Kakudmi bows and reads out his list of possible husbands. And Brahma laughs.
screen: `A KING, A DAUGHTER, A LIST.` → `THEY WAIT FOR ONE SONG.` → `BRAHMA LAUGHS.`

segments.voice: Every man on your list, Brahma says, is gone, and their sons, and their grandsons, and their whole lines. While you waited for one song, twenty-seven great cycles of ages passed on earth. Go back and give her to Balarama, Krishna's brother. Kakudmi comes home to a changed world and does just that. Here's the teaching behind the joke. Hindus see time as vast, and turning. Four ages, the yugas, make one great cycle, and the Gita says a day of Brahma lasts a thousand yugas, which teachers read as a thousand of those great cycles; then a night, then a new creation. Not a line from start to finish, but a wheel. Time itself, Kala, is a face of God: in the Gita, Krishna says, I am time. Then Patanjali adds something startling. Sutra 3.52: rest samyama on the instant and its sequence, and discerning knowledge is born. The classical commentary says the instant, kshana, is the smallest piece of time, as the atom is of matter, and that hours, days and ages are put together by the mind. Only one instant is real at a time. Brahma's day and Kakudmi's song are both made of instants. Sutra 3.54 names the knowledge that sees this: taraka, the one that carries across, like a ferry over the river of becoming. So the two ideas meet. Time is huge, a wheel of ages, and you only ever live one instant of it. A Hindu can hold a cosmos billions of years old and this one breath in the same hand.
screen: `TWENTY-SEVEN GREAT CYCLES, ONE SONG.` · `FOUR YUGAS, ONE CYCLE.` · `A THOUSAND CYCLES, ONE DAY OF BRAHMA.` · `KSHANA: THE SMALLEST PIECE OF TIME.` · `TARAKA: THE ONE THAT CARRIES ACROSS.` · then, large: `TIME IS A WHEEL OF AGES, LIVED ONE INSTANT AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus pray with a mala, a string of a hundred and eight beads, one name of God for each bead. Today let each bead, or each breath if you don't have one, be one instant: this touch of air, this name, then the next. When the mind builds something bigger, the rest of the week, the rest of the year, notice the building, and come back to this single bead.
Taraka, the knowledge that carries across, like a ferry over a river. It comes from seeing the instant clearly, and Hindu prayers use the same picture: crossing the ocean of becoming.
Your line: time is a wheel of ages, lived one instant at a time. That's day four seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Hindus describe time as vast and cyclical, with yugas and days of Brahma, and many pray with a japa mala of 108 beads, one name at a time; students of the Yoga Sutras read 3.52–3.54 with the commentary's account of the instant.

fork.setup: a friend says time is a straight line: one beginning, one end. what would a Hindu add from Kakudmi's story?
options: nothing; that's the Hindu view too.
time turns in cycles of ages, and it runs differently in Brahma's world.
time isn't real at all, so nothing matters.
fork.reveal: Hindus see time as a wheel of yugas, and Kakudmi's one song was ages on earth. Patanjali adds that only the instant is real. that doesn't mean nothing matters: the instant is where you live.

original.note: Sanskrit yuga: an age; four yugas make one great cycle, and the Gita's day of Brahma lasts a thousand yugas (8.17), read as a thousand great cycles.
